segments.script_text: That's Angela Maggard.
She said that into an open microphone on X—in a live audio room she had titled Logan Black Unmasked.
I'm Logan Black.

When Angela hosted that broadcast in September of 2026, she was speaking to hundreds of listeners in an online audio community where she had spent the last two years building a following as a whistle-blower and a fierce advocate for trauma survivors.
Over the course of that afternoon—and across weeks of broadcasts that surrounded it—she turned her microphone on me, and on the people closest to me.
If you tuned into those broadcasts as a stranger, you would think Angela was confronting an enemy she had been tracking from a distance.
What you wouldn't know is that for more than two years before that broadcast, Angela and I were friends.
Here is how Angela herself described our history just ten days earlier:
When Angela entered our community, she presented herself as a protector of vulnerable people—someone who fought for abused women and children and stood up to bullies.
People trusted her. I trusted her.
And so did a woman named Sav.
Sav was a mother who had become one of Angela's closest friends in our online community. They talked regularly about their children, their personal struggles, and the things going on in their lives.
Sav believed she had found someone she could confide in. Someone who understood her.
And like me, she had no idea how much that trust would eventually cost her.

When Angela turned on us in September, I started going through the recordings from thirty-five public broadcasts and the private messages behind them. I also started talking to the people Angela had been close to before us—people whose warnings I had dismissed when Angela and I were still on good terms.
And as I laid the recordings out in chronological order, two things became clear.

As I listened to former friends describing these conflicts, I had to keep one thing clear: for most of the calls to relatives, child-protection visits and alleged legal consequences, I don't have the original agency files or phone records. These are personal accounts, many from people who were already angry with Angela. They're not all independent proof of what she did.
But they do tell us what the people who trusted her say they experienced—and how those friendships broke apart.
Cambian describes one of those turning points: the moment he says Angela's praise became a demand for loyalty.
What Cambian describes is a shift in the rules of friendship. Agree with Angela and you're an ally. Refuse to join a campaign and, in his account, you're suddenly part of the enemy.
Other former friends described the consequences extending well beyond a microphone.

Peach was a mother in a group that included Angela, Timmy and Glow Baby. They say she was struggling when the friendships fractured. They also say Angela demanded that Peach choose sides, and that calls to her family and welfare checks followed.
Glow Baby believed those calls were a way to exert pressure. Angela's stated concern for a person's safety is a competing explanation we have to take seriously.
Here is how Glow Baby described what happened.
In Glow Baby's telling, the calls weren't the end of the friendship. They were one of the ways the falling-out reached Peach's family.
Timmy was part of that circle too. He alleged more serious things: private information being exposed, family contact, and calls to authorities.
But the thread that connects his account to the others is what he says Angela learned about survivors while they still trusted her—and what he believes happened after the friendships broke down.
That is Timmy's central allegation: getting close to survivors, learning their personal vulnerabilities, and later using what had been confided.
Glow Baby described what she says happened to her own family's information.

When former friends accused her of exposing private information, I had only their testimony. Here, I could hear Angela accept responsibility for helping expose it—though not proof that she was responsible for every other allegation.
And one of the people who had trusted Angela with painful details of her own life was Sav.
Go back to August, before the September broadcasts.

Sav was already going through a separation and trying to keep a home for her children. She had trusted Angela with the parts of her life she wasn't comfortable discussing in public—including arguments and insecurities in her relationship with me.
According to Sav, the immediate crisis began when Angela shared screenshots Sav had specifically asked her not to send. That triggered a fight between Sav and me. We blocked each other.
Sav was overwhelmed. She was crying and sending incoherent messages in a group chat with Angela and their friend Sara Beth. She also made alarming statements about ending her life.
Sav has acknowledged that those words were serious and that she shouldn't have used them lightly.
She called Sara Beth to calm down. Sav says Sara Beth helped her through the panic, and that both of them told Angela she was okay.
Angela nonetheless believed a police welfare check was necessary. While I was at work, Sara Beth asked me for Sav's address on Angela's behalf. I gave it to her because I wanted to know Sav was safe.
When Sara Beth told Sav that a welfare check was being called, Sav says she was overwhelmed again—after the friend she'd called for help had already talked her through the initial panic.
She still had children in the house. She needed them to know what was about to happen without frightening them more.
In a written statement she provided for this documentary, Sav described what that moment felt like. These are her words, read aloud from the statement:
Sav says she spoke to the officer with Sara Beth still on the phone. Then the police left.

We have to keep two questions separate. Was a check reasonable after a message suggesting someone might end their life? It could have been. Angela has said she was afraid for Sav and knew calling might cost their friendship.

But Sav says the call went ahead after both she and Sara Beth told Angela she had calmed down. Sav believed the way it was handled was connected to the online dispute, and that she was being taught a lesson.
That is Sav's interpretation. I cannot know Angela's private motive from the accounts we have.
What I can do is follow what happened to information from that night. Because the story didn't end when the officer left.
Within weeks, Angela was describing disappointment with people she considered friends. On September 7, she named Sine and me while explaining why she believed others had failed her.
The next day, on September 8, Angela began a broadcast in which she announced that she was going to post private relationship messages.
And that is where the personal crisis Sav had described became part of something much bigger.
By the beginning of September, private conversations were already making their way into public Spaces. And people were nervous about getting involved.
The Space was what the audience heard. The back channels—private messages, group chats, and Discord rooms—were where people said things they never expected that audience to hear.

On September 2, I talked about screenshots I believed Angela had posted. I asked another host to hide them. He wouldn't—and the reason he gave says something about how powerful her reputation had become.
You'll hear his refusal described in my own words, followed by another speaker who starts to explain why he wanted no part of the conflict.
“Because they told her secrets and they can never—”
He stops there. The rest of that thought isn't recorded. But the fear in the conversation is hard to miss.

By then, even other hosts were afraid of what might happen if they crossed Angela. Six days later, something happened in my own room that Angela would use to explain why she was releasing even more private messages.
In another recorded confrontation, Angela defended her decision to request the police welfare check at Sav's home.
Her explanation matters. She said she feared for Sav's safety, understood that the call might end their friendship, and made it anyway.
"Angela, shut the fuck up, Angela. Angela, shut up."
Angela may well have been genuinely frightened for Sav. Her explanation deserves to be heard in full.

But the welfare call and what happened to information from that day are two different questions. What did it mean to protect somebody when the most intimate details of their crisis could later enter an escalating argument?

On September 18, Sav spoke publicly. She acknowledged her own insecurity and involvement in private gossip, but she also asked listeners to understand what it felt like to have her personal life exposed.
After so many people had talked about her, it matters to hear her uninterrupted.
That is Sav describing how people caught up in an online conflict ended up carrying consequences in their real lives.

Then on September 30, Angela hosted a Space about the social cost of taking a suicide threat seriously. She spoke about the possibility that authorities or family members might encounter the messages.
That is her public position.

What appeared in a later private group chat needs to be considered separately, because those messages went further—and the identity of the person operating the account has not been independently confirmed.
The screenshots show a conversation in a women's group chat, with a Monday-morning timestamp.

The account on the screen is labelled “Angela's Spaces Alt.” That is what the screenshots show; the account label alone does not prove who was typing. The exact calendar date is also not printed in the visible morning exchange.
I want you to understand the distinction before you hear the words. This is a reading of written messages, not an authenticated recording of Angela speaking.
At 6:35 in the morning, the labelled account discussed a recording of Sav while she was in distress, with her children in the background.

If Sav's account is accurate, the stakes of confiding in Angela were no longer just whether a screenshot would be posted in a public room. They extended to the people Sav relied on outside the internet.

And that is the part of this story I find hardest to dismiss: the very circumstances that made people seek somebody's help could, after a falling-out, become the details they most feared being exposed.
Think about the people who entered this story.
Sine believed he was sending survivors to an advocate. Later, he said he feared he had been directing them toward someone who would target them.
Glow Baby and Timmy described friendships that, in their telling, led to threats and private family information being used in disputes. Some of those claims still lack independent corroboration.

Sav believed she had a friend she could be honest with about motherhood, insecurity and a life that was coming apart. Then she heard private details from that life recast in public, and said the conflict reached her family.
And Angela?

In her own recordings, she described gathering information before approaching people, saving screenshots, keeping names and documents in reserve, and helping expose information when she believed she was justified.
She also said there were limits. She said you shouldn't release something just to twist the knife. She said some evidence could be weaponized.
Then she described the point where she decided to release it anyway.

I can't tell you everything Angela believed. I can't turn every accusation made about her into an established fact. But I can put the explanations she gave beside what the people who trusted her say they experienced.
That was the promise of this investigation. Not that a microphone can read somebody's mind. That the words people choose—and the consequences others describe—can be heard together.
Angela once invited listeners to do exactly that. To believe the good things they heard about her, and the bad, and make up their own minds.
I'll leave you with her invitation.
